Pretty much everything in *NIX is a file. Your hard drives, CD/DVD, thumbdrives, etc. are files in /dev. They're special files, sure, but they're still files. You can cat random_file.txt > /dev/audio, which will send the contents of random_file.txt to the audio device and create noise over your speakers. (You probably won't have a /dev/audio, old example).

Most of the heavy lifting done in Linux is via command line apps. This is changing, but for the most part, graphical apps are just wrappers around command line apps. If you're familiar with those command line apps, you can accomplish tasks in less time than it takes to fire up most GUI counterparts. For instance, you can run K3B to burn a DVD, or :

growisofs -dvd-compat -Z /dev/sr0=/path/to/DiskImage.iso

You can fire up a music player and play music or:

mpg123 -Z /path/to/*.mp3

and randomly play a directory full of mp3's.

The other is I am not sure what a console editor is and what it can be used for

Since most of Linux is command line programs, most of their configuration is done via plain text file. If you want to administer a system, you're going to have to change these text files. You can use graphical text editors. There's a ton of them (Kate, Kedit, Gedit, Nedit, Geany, Mousepad, Medit, etc.) and they work fine.

What happens when you have to work on a remote system, like a raspberry pi over a SSH connection?

You can set up X11 forwarding, remotedesktop or VNC to fire up a text editor on a graphical desktop on a remote machine, but it's sloooow. Plus, you may not have the rights for X11 forwarding on the remote machine, or to install a graphical desktop. Now you have to use a text editor that works in a terminal over a text-based connection.

Now, you might want to use an editor that would work quickly in this text-based environment. Vim, Emacs or nano is the text editors you want to use here. You can use these editors in a terminal to edit anything you would use a graphical text editor to edit.

They have graphical counterparts (gVim for Vim, XEmacs for Emacs). They have plugins to help simplify editing of files beyond plain old text files. Emacs can do so much it's nearly its own operating system. They're very powerful, but they're not very intuitive for beginners.

Derek Wyatt has some excellent Vim video tutorials if you want to give Vim a try. I like Vim more because it's still very powerful out of the box with no customization. Vi, Vim's predecessor, was written to be usable over a 300 baud modem.

Jess Hamrick has a pretty good absolute beginners guide to Emacs. If you get good with Emacs, you'll learn readline shortcuts, and readline shortcuts are useful pretty much everywhere in the terminal. Emacs is more powerful after you get it customized the way you want it, which is fine on your machine, if your ssh'ed into another machine, maybe not so much.

I've written bash scripts to:

  • Download podcasts
  • Write a blog
  • Change my background to a random wallpaper
  • Download weather alerts and push them to my phone (I get crappy data reception where I work)
  • Mass convert videos to HTML5 compliant files (mp4, webm and ogv)
  • Batch tag mp3 files based on file names
  • Mass rename mp3 files based on id3 tags
  • Have my computer remind me it's time to go with text-to-speech announcing the appointment and stating the current time
  • Download my agenda from Google Calendar, print today's events in new terminal windows and remind me it's time to go (see above)

All of this is done by stringing command line tools together, putting them in a script file and executing them according to a schedule with cron. Most of those programs come stock with every Linux distribution. They're ugly, quick, easily customizable to your specific situation and will familiarize you with your operating system.
